# Combinatorics {#sec-Combinatorics}
Combinatorics is the branch of mathematics that studies the counting, arrangement, and combination of objects. It provides tools and techniques for solving problems related to counting and arranging objects in numerous ways. Combinatorics is fundamental in probability theory, as it helps determine the number of possible outcomes in a given experiment. In @exm-Coin_Toss the probability of getting a certain number of heads in a series of coin tosses is derived. This example uses combinatorics to derive the number of ways we can arrange the heads and tails in the series of tosses. This principle can be extended to more complex scenarios, such as calculating the probability of drawing a certain hand in a card game or the probability of a specific outcome in a dice roll.


## Multiplication Principle {#sec-Multiplication_Principle}
The multiplication principle is the foundation of combinatorics, which is why it is so important. It states that if one action can be performed in $m$ ways, and a second independent action can be performed in $n$ ways, then the two actions can be performed together in $m \cdot n$ ways. More generally, if we have a sequence of $k$ independent choices, where the $i$th choice can be made in $n_i$ ways, then the total number of possible outcomes is
$$
n_1 \cdot n_2 \cdots n_k = \prod_{i = 1}^k n_i.
$$

For example, when tossing a coin as in @exm-Coin_Toss, each toss has $2$ possible outcomes, so the total number of outcomes for five tosses is $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 2^5 = 32$, matching the size of the sample space $\Omega$.


## Permutations {#sec-Permutations}
A permutation is an arrangement of outcomes in a specific order, meaning that the order in which the outcomes appear matters. If we have $n$ distinct outcomes and want to arrange all of them, there are $n$ choices for the first position, $n - 1$ choices for the second position, and so on, until only a single outcome remains for the last position. By the multiplication principle, the number of ways to order $n$ distinct outcomes is therefore $n!$ ($n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot (n - 2) \cdots 1$). More often we are interested in ordering only $k$ of the $n$ available outcomes. Following the same reasoning, there are $n$ choices for the first position, $n - 1$ for the second, down to $n - k + 1$ for the $k$th position. The number of such ordered arrangements, denoted $P(n, k)$, is
$$
P(n, k) = \frac{n!}{(n - k)!}, \quad 0 \leq k \leq n.
$${#eq-Permutations}
For example, the number of ways to award gold, silver, and bronze medals among 8 runners is $P(8, 3) = \frac{8!}{5!} = 336$, since the order matters.

### Permutations with Repetition {#sec-Permutations_with_Repetition}
When some of the outcomes are identical, several orderings become indistinguishable, and the count $n!$ overcounts the number of distinct arrangements. Suppose we arrange $n$ outcomes that fall into $k$ groups of identical outcomes, with $n_1$ outcomes of the first kind, $n_2$ of the second kind, and so on, where $\sum_{i = 1}^k n_i = n$. Each distinct arrangement is counted $\prod_{i = 1}^k n_i!$ times in $n!$, since permuting identical outcomes among themselves does not produce a new arrangement. The number of distinct permutations is then
$$
\binom{n}{n_1, n_2, \dots, n_k} = \frac{n!}{n_1! \cdot n_2! \cdots n_k!}.
$$
This quantity is called the multinomial coefficient. Returning to @exm-Coin_Toss, the number of ways to arrange $k$ heads and $n - k$ tails in a sequence of $n$ tosses is $\frac{n!}{k! \cdot (n - k)!}$, which is exactly the count needed to determine the probability of observing $k$ heads.


## Combinations {#sec-Combinations}
A combination is a selection of objects where the order does not matter, in contrast to a permutation. When choosing $k$ objects out of $n$ distinct objects without regard to order, each unordered selection corresponds to $k!$ different ordered arrangements. Dividing the number of permutations in @eq-Permutations by $k!$ removes this ordering, giving the number of combinations
$$
\binom{n}{k} = \frac{P(n, k)}{k!} = \frac{n!}{k! \cdot (n - k)!}, \quad 0 \leq k \leq n.
$$ {#eq-Binomial_Coefficient}
This quantity is known as the binomial coefficient and is read as "$n$ choose $k$". For example, the number of ways to draw a hand of 5 cards from a standard deck of 52 is $\binom{52}{5} = 2598960$, since the order in which the cards are drawn is irrelevant.

::: {.callout-tip collapse = true title = "Binomial Coefficient Properties" #tip-Binomial_Coefficient_Properties}
For non-negative integers $n$ and $k$ with $0 \leq k \leq n$, the binomial coefficient satisfies
$$
\begin{aligned}
    \binom{n}{k} &= \binom{n}{n - k} \\
    \binom{n}{0} &= \binom{n}{n} = 1 \\
    \binom{n}{k} &= \binom{n - 1}{k - 1} + \binom{n - 1}{k} \\
    \sum_{k = 0}^n \binom{n}{k} &= 2^n
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

### Combinations with Repetition {#sec-Combinations_with_Repetition}
In some situations we select $k$ objects from $n$ distinct types, where each type may be chosen more than once and the order of selection still does not matter. This is known as a combination with repetition, or drawing with replacement. A classic example is choosing $k$ scoops of ice cream from $n$ available flavours, where flavours may be repeated. The number of such selections is
$$
\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n + k - 1}{k} = \frac{(n + k - 1)!}{k! \cdot (n - 1)!}.
$$
This result follows from the stars and bars argument, where the $k$ selected objects are represented as stars and the $n - 1$ dividers separating the $n$ types are represented as bars, giving $n + k - 1$ symbols in total from which the $k$ star positions are chosen. For example, the number of ways to choose 3 scoops from 5 flavours is $\binom{5 + 3 - 1}{3} = \binom{7}{3} = 35$.
